widgetTypes.description: The one KPI card: a short title (a few words: put units and qualifiers such as "month to date" in `description`, not in the title), a large value, an optional description line and an optional trend (the delta, with an arrow that is green when the change is good and red when it is bad). Use one `metric` per number; consecutive `metric` widgets sit side by side in one row. Put a per-entity breakdown (per machine, per shift) in a `table` or chart, not in a KPI card.

fields.doc: Dot-path into the run output payload, e.g. "totals.revenue".

Optional dot-path to a delta/comparison number, shown at the right of the description line with a trend arrow. Positive shows an up arrow with a "+", negative a down arrow; the color follows `good_direction`. With "percent" format, give a 0-1 fraction (0.5 shows +50%).
Which way the delta is an improvement: "up" (default, e.g. throughput) turns a rise green and a fall red; "down" (e.g. delays, cost) the opposite.
Optional fixed line of context under the value, e.g. "vs last week". Use `description_key` instead when the text comes from the run output.
Optional dot-path to a string in the run output shown as the description line, e.g. "5 of 65 ops". Wins over `description` when the path resolves.
Display format. "currency" is USD; "percent" expects a 0-1 fraction.
Suffix appended to a "number"-formatted value, e.g. "kg".

widgetTypes.tomlExample:
[[widgets]]
type = "metric"
id = "revenue"
title = "Total revenue"
value_key = "totals.revenue"
format = "currency"
delta_key = "totals.revenue_change"
description = "vs last week"

widgetTypes.description: A sortable data grid bound to an array of row objects.

fields.doc: Dot-path to an array of row objects in the run output payload.
One or more `{ key, label? }` entries, in display order. `key` is a top-level field on each row (not a dot-path).
Optional one-line explanation shown under the title in the card header, e.g. "Daily operational schedule". Keep the title short and put the detail here.

widgetTypes.tomlExample:
[[widgets]]
type = "table"
id = "breakdown"
title = "Breakdown"
rows_key = "breakdown"
columns = [
  { key = "name", label = "Name" },
  { key = "value", label = "Value" },
]

widgetTypes.description: A flat treemap — one rectangle per row, area proportional to `value_key`, labeled from `name_key`. Good for a breakdown where relative size matters more than exact values (e.g. cost by machine).

fields.doc: Dot-path to the array of row objects to size rectangles from.
Row field sized into each rectangle's area. Rows with a missing or non-positive value are dropped.
Row field shown as each rectangle's label.
Row field grouped into a stable color per distinct value. Omit for one palette color per rectangle in source order.

Pins specific `color_key` values to specific colors, e.g. `colors = { "Late job" = "red-600", "Unassigned" = { light = "neutral-400", dark = "neutral-600" } }`. Every other value still cycles through the default grays (skipping any color pinned here). Leave color unset unless the user asks for one: unset colors render as neutral grays that adapt to light/dark mode, which is the default look. When the user does ask, use a Tailwind color name (`<family>-<shade>`, e.g. `green-300`, `red-600`, or `black`/`white` — see the schema's `colorNames`), never hex. A single name is used as-is in both themes; prefer a `{ light = "...", dark = "..." }` pair (e.g. a darker shade for light mode and a lighter one for dark mode) so it reads on both backgrounds.

Dot-path to a total-capacity number (e.g. total yard positions). When the rows' summed value_key is less than this, a synthetic "Free" tile fills the remainder, so area doubles as a capacity gauge. Omitted, or at/below the summed value, adds no tile.
Optional one-line explanation shown under the title in the card header, e.g. "Daily operational schedule". Keep the title short and put the detail here.

widgetTypes.tomlExample:
[[widgets]]
type = "treemap"
id = "cost-breakdown"
title = "Cost by machine"
items_key = "breakdown"
value_key = "cost"
name_key = "machine"

widgetTypes.description: An entity x time-bucket grid, shaded by intensity — one row per resource, one column per bucket (e.g. hour of day). A `(resource, bucket)` pair with no matching row renders as a distinct unavailable cell rather than a zero.

fields.doc: Dot-path to the array of row objects to grid. One row per `(resource, bucket)` pair that has a value — a pair with no row renders as unavailable, not zero.
Row field naming the resource/machine its row belongs to. Defaults to "resource".
Row field naming the time bucket (e.g. an hour number) its row belongs to. Defaults to "bucket".
Row field shaded into cell intensity. Defaults to "value".
Suffix appended to a cell's tooltip value, e.g. "cycles".
Optional one-line explanation shown under the title in the card header, e.g. "Daily operational schedule". Keep the title short and put the detail here.

widgetTypes.tomlExample:
[[widgets]]
type = "heatmap"
id = "hourly-cycles"
title = "Cycles per hour"
items_key = "hourly_cycles"
resource_key = "resource"
bucket_key = "bucket"
value_key = "value"

widgetTypes.description: Line, bar, area, scatter, pie or donut, picked by `variant` — one widget for every chart picture, so changing how data is drawn never means changing the widget. Optionally split rows into colored groups with `group_key`, stack them with `stack`, lay bars on their side with `orientation`, and mix marks per series (bars plus a line) with `series[].mark`. It replaces `line-chart` and `bar-chart`, which are still accepted in existing files.

fields.doc: Which picture to draw. "line" or "area" for a value trending over time; "bar" for comparing categories (add `orientation = "horizontal"` when the labels are long); "pie" or "donut" only for the parts of one whole with at most about six slices (a seventh and beyond are folded into "Other" past eight); "scatter" for the relationship between two numbers. Changing it never needs a different widget.
Dot-path to an array of data points in the run output payload.
The data point field to use as the category/x-axis value. For "pie"/"donut" it is each slice's label; for "scatter" it must hold numbers.

One or more `{ key, label?, color?, mark? }` entries — each renders as its own line/bar/area/point set (a "pie"/"donut" draws only the first). `mark` (`line`, `bar` or `area`) overrides the chart's `variant` for that one series, which is how to draw bars plus a line on the same axis. Leave color unset unless the user asks for one: unset colors render as neutral grays that adapt to light/dark mode, which is the default look. When the user does ask, use a Tailwind color name (`<family>-<shade>`, e.g. `green-300`, `red-600`, or `black`/`white` — see the schema's `colorNames`), never hex. A single name is used as-is in both themes; prefer a `{ light = "...", dark = "..." }` pair (e.g. a darker shade for light mode and a lighter one for dark mode) so it reads on both backgrounds. Examples: `color = "green-600"`, `color = { light = "blue-700", dark = "blue-300" }`.

For long-format data (one row per category and group): the row field whose distinct values each become their own series, valued by `series[0].key`. Use it instead of listing one series per group; combine with `stack` to stack the groups.

"stacked" piles bar/area series on top of each other; "percent" normalizes every category to 100%. Needs bar/area series only (a "percent" chart with a line series falls back to "stacked"). Defaults to "none".
"horizontal" lays bars on their side so long category labels stay readable. Only for bar charts (every series a bar); ignored otherwise. Defaults to "vertical".
How a line or area joins its points: "smooth" (the default), "linear" for straight segments, "step" for values that hold until the next change.
Orders categories (bar) or slices (pie/donut) by value — by `series[0]`, or by the category's total when `group_key` is set. "none" (the default) keeps the source order. Leave unset for a time axis.
Number format for the value axis and tooltips. "currency" is USD; "percent" expects a 0-1 fraction.
Suffix appended to a "number"-formatted value, e.g. "kg".
Title shown under the category (x) axis.
Title shown beside the value (y) axis.

Pins a pie/donut slice (by its `x_key` value) or a `group_key` group to a color, e.g. `colors = { "Late" = "red-600" }`. Every other slice or group still cycles the default grays. Leave color unset unless the user asks for one: unset colors render as neutral grays that adapt to light/dark mode, which is the default look. When the user does ask, use a Tailwind color name (`<family>-<shade>`, e.g. `green-300`, `red-600`, or `black`/`white` — see the schema's `colorNames`), never hex. A single name is used as-is in both themes; prefer a `{ light = "...", dark = "..." }` pair (e.g. a darker shade for light mode and a lighter one for dark mode) so it reads on both backgrounds.
Optional one-line explanation shown under the title in the card header, e.g. "Daily operational schedule". Keep the title short and put the detail here.

widgetTypes.tomlExample:
[[widgets]]
type = "chart"
id = "trend"
title = "Objective value over time"
variant = "line"
data_key = "timeseries"
x_key = "label"
series = [{ key = "value", label = "Objective value" }]

widgetTypes.description: A resource-row Gantt chart on a numeric time axis — the common shape for scheduling/job-shop solver results (one row per machine/resource, one bar per task).

fields.doc: Dot-path to an array of task objects in the run output payload.
Task field naming the resource/machine its row is grouped under. Defaults to "resource".
Task field for its display label. Defaults to "task".
Task field for its numeric start time. Defaults to "start".
Task field for its numeric end time. Set either this or `duration_key` — `end_key` wins when both are set, and a task resolving neither is dropped from the chart.
Task field for a numeric duration, added to `start_key`, for solvers that emit start+duration. Read only when `end_key` is unset.
Task field naming a categorical group (e.g. a job spanning several tasks), colored from a stable palette.

Pins specific `color_key` values to specific colors, e.g. `colors = { "Late job" = "red-600", "Unassigned" = { light = "neutral-400", dark = "neutral-600" } }`. Every other value still cycles through the default grays (skipping any color pinned here). Leave color unset unless the user asks for one: unset colors render as neutral grays that adapt to light/dark mode, which is the default look. When the user does ask, use a Tailwind color name (`<family>-<shade>`, e.g. `green-300`, `red-600`, or `black`/`white` — see the schema's `colorNames`), never hex. A single name is used as-is in both themes; prefer a `{ light = "...", dark = "..." }` pair (e.g. a darker shade for light mode and a lighter one for dark mode) so it reads on both backgrounds.

How start/end/duration values are read: a plain display suffix (e.g. "min"), or a wall-clock sentinel — "epoch" (seconds since epoch), "epoch_ms" (milliseconds), or "iso" (an ISO 8601 string) — rendered as a real time instead of a bare number.
Optional one-line explanation shown under the title in the card header, e.g. "Daily operational schedule". Keep the title short and put the detail here.

widgetTypes.tomlExample:
[[widgets]]
type = "gantt-chart"
id = "schedule"
title = "Machine schedule"
tasks_key = "schedule"
time_unit = "min"

widgetTypes.description: A resource-row timeline on a numeric time axis. Supersedes `gantt-chart`: interrupted work folds into one item drawn with gaps, non-working spans render as background bands, the axis is drag-to-zoom, a `[clock]` playhead shows as a now-marker, and rows it cannot draw are reported instead of silently dropped.

fields.doc: Dot-path to an array of interval objects in the run output payload.
Item field naming the resource/machine its row is grouped under. Defaults to "resource".
Item field for its display label. Defaults to "task".
Item field for its numeric start time. Defaults to "start".
Item field for its numeric end time. Set either this or `duration_key` — `end_key` wins when both are set.
Item field for a numeric duration, added to `start_key`, for solvers that emit start+duration. Read only when `end_key` is unset.
Item field naming a categorical group, colored from a stable palette.

Pins specific `color_key` values to specific colors, e.g. `colors = { "Late job" = "red-600", "Unassigned" = { light = "neutral-400", dark = "neutral-600" } }`. Every other value still cycles through the default grays (skipping any color pinned here). Leave color unset unless the user asks for one: unset colors render as neutral grays that adapt to light/dark mode, which is the default look. When the user does ask, use a Tailwind color name (`<family>-<shade>`, e.g. `green-300`, `red-600`, or `black`/`white` — see the schema's `colorNames`), never hex. A single name is used as-is in both themes; prefer a `{ light = "...", dark = "..." }` pair (e.g. a darker shade for light mode and a lighter one for dark mode) so it reads on both backgrounds.

Item field identifying the logical task a row belongs to. Rows sharing a value on one resource fold into a single interrupted item drawn with gaps, instead of separate bars that hide the fact they are one job.
Dot-path to an array of non-working spans (off-shift, maintenance), drawn as background bands.
Region field for its numeric start. Defaults to "start".
Region field for its numeric end. Defaults to "end".
Region field for a label shown on hover.
Region field naming the single resource it applies to. Regions without one apply to every row.

How start/end/duration (and region) values are read: a plain display suffix (e.g. "min"), or a wall-clock sentinel — "epoch" (seconds since epoch), "epoch_ms" (milliseconds), or "iso" (an ISO 8601 string) — rendered as a real time instead of a bare number.
Optional one-line explanation shown under the title in the card header, e.g. "Daily operational schedule". Keep the title short and put the detail here.

widgetTypes.tomlExample:
[[widgets]]
type = "timeline"
id = "schedule"
title = "Machine schedule"
items_key = "schedule"
id_key = "op"
regions_key = "breaks"
time_unit = "min"

widgetTypes.description: Geocoded points and/or routes on a real-world basemap — vehicle routing, delivery stops, facility locations.

fields.doc: Dot-path to an array of point row objects in the run output payload. Omit for a routes-only map.
Point row field for its numeric latitude. Defaults to "lat".
Point row field for its numeric longitude. Defaults to "lng".
Point row field for its display label, shown on hover/click.
Point row field identifying it for the shared dashboard selection. Falls back to the label, then to source order, when unset.
Point row field naming a categorical group, colored from a stable palette — e.g. which vehicle a stop is assigned to.
Dot-path to an array of route row objects in the run output payload. Omit for a points-only map.
Route row field naming its ordered stop sequence — an array of `[lat, lng]` pairs or `{ lat, lng }` objects. Defaults to "path".
Route row field naming a categorical group, colored from a stable palette — e.g. which vehicle drove the route.

`https://` XYZ raster tile template (`{s}`/`{z}`/`{x}`/`{y}` placeholders); any other scheme falls back to the default. Defaults to OpenStreetMap's public tile servers — swap for a self-hosted tile server in a locked-down deployment. Every viewer of the dashboard, including anonymous share-link viewers, requests tiles from this host.
Plain-text attribution shown in the map's corner (HTML is escaped, not rendered). Defaults to OpenStreetMap's, matching the default `tile_url`.
Optional one-line explanation shown under the title in the card header, e.g. "Daily operational schedule". Keep the title short and put the detail here.

widgetTypes.tomlExample:
[[widgets]]
type = "map"
id = "routes"
title = "Delivery routes"
points_key = "stops"
label_key = "label"
color_key = "vehicle"
routes_key = "routes"
route_color_key = "vehicle"
